Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital payment systems.  21 variables in 4 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: Partial evidence: Egypt has a general Consumer Protection Law No. 181 of 2018 covering consumer rights including e-commerce; CBE mobile payments regulations referenced by AFI recommend service contracts with transparent terms & conditions, defined rights/obligations, service availability/SLA notices, data confidentiality, and dispute resolution controls for mobile payment services. ([Riad & Riad on Consumer Protection Law 181/2018](https://riad-riad.com/new-egyptian-consumer-protection-law/);[AFI 'Financial Inclusion through DFS & Fintech: the case of Egypt'](https://www.afi-global.org/sites/default/files/publications/2018-08/AFI_Egypt_Report_AW_digital.pdf))
revision_notes: Fetched both originally cited sources: the Riad & Riad note only summarises the general Consumer Protection Law 181/2018 and does not address payment-specific rules; the AFI 2018 PDF is a broad financial-inclusion case study contributed by the CBE and does not itself set out payment-specific consumer protection provisions in the detail the comment implies. A fresh search surfaced stronger, more specific and more current authority: the Central Bank and Banking Sector Law No. 194 of 2020 gives the CBE explicit statutory power to set customer protection, disclosure and dispute-settlement rules for payment system operators and payment service providers (Articles 184-199, 201, 205-206, 216, 225), and current legal commentary (Chambers and Partners Fintech 2026 Egypt guide, updated March 2026) confirms that the general Consumer Protection Law does NOT apply to CBE-regulated payment entities - instead CBE's own dedicated regime governs. CBE's 'Instructions for the Protection of the Rights of Bank Customers' (19 February 2019, per Shalakany Law Office) explicitly extend to providers of mobile payment services and mandate a dedicated complaints unit with a 15-day response requirement and a right of escalation to the CBE. This is a dedicated, payment-specific consumer protection framework rather than reliance on general consumer law, meeting the scale's 'Yes' threshold. Recalculated value code raised from 2 (Partial) to 3 (Yes), the top of this variable's scale, so flagged for human review per protocol notwithstanding the multiple corroborating authoritative legal-practice sources (Chambers and Partners, Shalakany, Andersen, Lexology).
revised_comments: Egypt's Central Bank and Banking Sector Law No. 194 of 2020 establishes a dedicated payment-specific consumer protection regime for entities licensed by the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE), including payment system operators and payment service providers. It sets out customer protection, dispute settlement, pricing disclosure and service-quality obligations (Articles 184-199, 201, 205-206, 216 and 225), and the general Consumer Protection Law No. 181 of 2018 explicitly does not apply to CBE-regulated payment institutions. In addition, the CBE's 'Instructions for the Protection of the Rights of Bank Customers' (19 February 2019) apply to banks and providers of banking and mobile payment services, requiring fair and transparent dealing, clear contract terms, disclosure of fees and interest rates, and a dedicated complaints unit that must respond within 15 days, with a right of escalation to the CBE. Egypt's Instant Payment Network (Instapay), operating under CBE oversight since 2022, runs a dispute resolution system requiring participant banks to maintain auditable transaction trails to support fraud investigations and complaint resolution.
